caption: Why is 10,000 steps the holy fitness number? The surprising 1965 origin story and what medical science actually reveals.
youtube_title: Where Did 10,000 Steps Actually Come From?
youtube_description:
Marcus is pacing circles around his living room at midnight, desperate to hit 10,000 steps. But where did that 5-digit target actually come from?

It wasn't a medical discovery. Ahead of the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, a Japanese clock company released the 'Manpo-kei' pedometer in 1965—picking 10,000 because the kanji character (万) looks like a walking person. It was a marketing gimmick, not biology.

Modern research from Harvard (JAMA Internal Medicine, 2019) and a 15-cohort meta-analysis in The Lancet Public Health (2022) reveals that longevity benefits level off around 7,500 steps per day. Walking more is great, but sacrificing your sleep to pace late at night just burns recovery.

Sources:
1. Lee IM, et al. (2019). Association of Step Volume and Intensity With All-Cause Mortality in Older Healthcare Women. JAMA Intern Med, 179(8):1105-1112. DOI: 10.1001/jamainternmed.2019.1664
2. Paluch AE, et al. (2022). Daily steps and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of 15 international cohorts. Lancet Public Health, 7(3):e219-e228. DOI: 10.1016/S2468-2667(21)00302-9

Silence the tracker, take care of your sleep, and keep moving.
